metadata.title: School efficiency in Latin America before and after the COVID-19 pandemic: New evidence from PISA 2018 and 2022

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA 2018 and PISA 2022 microdata merged at the school level (pooled working sample of 4,969 schools across nine Latin America and Caribbean countries). The analysis constructs DEA inputs/outputs using school-level averages and uses the first of ten plausible values for math, reading, and science as DEA outputs. The paper does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures in the DEA/second-stage regressions; instead, it relies on (i) homogeneous bootstrap for bias-correcting DEA efficiency scores and (ii) bootstrap replications for second-stage coefficient inference. Because the methodology is production-frontier/DEA-based rather than ML prediction, the manuscript does not document a complex-survey weighting variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT), so weighting strategy is unclear from the provided text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not describe any missing-data handling procedure for the school-level variables used in DEA and the second-stage regressions (e.g., whether cases with missing covariates were excluded or imputed). This is a reporting gap because PISA datasets typically contain missingness in questionnaire items and derived indices, and the study relies on many such covariates (e.g., ICT home resources, classroom climate, parental support). The absence of documentation prevents assessing potential bias from listwise deletion or imputation choices.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The working sample is restricted to the same nine LAC countries in both waves: Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Dominican Rep., Mexico, Panama, Peru, and Uruguay. The authors exclude Paraguay because it is not present in PISA 2018, and exclude Costa Rica because PISA 2022 lacks key family SES information needed for the DEA input formulation. The school-level dataset is constructed by merging student and school datasets and averaging key variables at the school level; DEA is run separately for PISA 2018 and PISA 2022, producing efficiency scores for each school. For DEA outputs, the study uses the first plausible value (PV1) out of ten for math, reading, and science. The paper does not report additional task-level completion filters or explicit missing-covariate exclusion rules in the provided text.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Average TEBC: 0.753 (95% CI: 0.730–0.774); bootstrap performance: 28.41; N schools: 2552.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 the study leveraged Gender (male share), IT home resources index, School type (private), Computer per student, and within-school inequality indicators to explain school technical efficiency (TEBC) via a two-stage DEA + bootstrap regression approach, finding that the region’s average efficiency remained statistically stable relative to 2022 (TEBC 0.753) and that efficiency determinants differed by wave (e.g., IT home resources index had a positive association in 2018). This indicates that pre-pandemic efficiency levels in LAC were not simply driven by a single student or school factor, but by a mix of household ICT access and school resource configuration, with associations rather than causal effects.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Average TEBC: 0.781 (95% CI: 0.761–0.800); bootstrap performance: 33.43; N schools: 2417.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 the study leveraged IT home resources index, School type (private), Computer per student, and within-school inequality indicators to explain school technical efficiency (TEBC), finding that the LAC region’s average efficiency was 0.781 and that efficiency could be increased by roughly 25% (22% keeping inputs constant) while the efficiency–equality trade-off did not hold empirically. This indicates that post-pandemic efficiency gains are compatible with equity-oriented strategies (e.g., reducing within-school inequality and exclusion), though the paper explicitly cautions that cross-sectional PISA limits causal interpretation.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 & 2022 (school-level) — inequality indicators as second-stage covariates
main_findings.performance_metrics: Inequality–efficiency (math): Gini ME = -0.1296 (2018) vs -0.1617 (2022); Level 1 or below ME = -0.2295 (2018) vs -0.2133 (2022); SES low-high ratio ME = -0.0069 (2018, not significant) vs -0.0289 (2022, p≤0.10); High achievers from bottom SES ME = 0.0799 (2018) vs 0.0825 (2022, p≤0.01).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 and PISA 2022 school-level inequality indicators, the study leveraged low performers (level 1 or below), within-school Gini, SES low-high ratio, and high achievers from bottom SES to predict school efficiency, finding that reducing within-school inequality and exclusion is associated with higher efficiency (e.g., Gini and level-1-or-below have negative marginal effects on efficiency). This indicates that equity-focused interventions that reduce learning dispersion and exclusion can simultaneously improve resource-to-achievement efficiency in LAC schools, even after COVID-19 disruptions.

main_findings.target_variable: School technical efficiency (TEBC) explained by pandemic factors
main_findings.performance_metrics: Pandemic covariates (Table 6): School support ME = 0.0105 (p≤0.01); Homework own digital device ME = 0.0913 (p≤0.01); Homework problem quiet place ME = -0.0245 (p≤0.01); Communication with teachers ME = 0.0175 (p≤0.01); Barriers for remote instruction ME = -0.0211 (p≤0.01).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 the study leveraged school support, homework own digital device, homework problem quiet place, communication with teachers, and barriers for remote instruction to predict school technical efficiency (TEBC), finding that engagement-support mechanisms and access to learning-enabling ICT are positively associated with efficiency while remote-instruction barriers and lack of a quiet study place are negatively associated. This indicates that post-pandemic efficiency improvements in LAC require both pedagogic engagement policies and targeted mitigation of digital and home-environment constraints, though the estimates remain correlational due to PISA’s cross-sectional design.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes school efficiency in Latin America and the Caribbean using OECD PISA 2018 and PISA 2022. It constructs school-level DEA production-frontier models where outputs are school-average math, reading, and science scores using PV1 (first of ten plausible values), and inputs include family SES, physical and educational school infrastructure, and the student–teacher ratio. The pooled working sample covers nine countries with 2,552 schools in 2018 and 2,417 schools in 2022. Average bias-corrected technical efficiency (TEBC) is 0.753 in 2018 and 0.781 in 2022, with overlapping confidence intervals, implying no statistical shift in regional efficiency. Second-stage bootstrap regressions show that efficiency is higher when within-school inequality and exclusion are lower (e.g., Gini and level-1-or-below have negative marginal effects), and that COVID-19 engagement/support policies and ICT access are positively associated with efficiency. Limitations include correlational (not causal) interpretation from cross-sectional PISA and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling and survey-weight usage.
